chapter: Swing, singers, Ed Fox and recordings
title: Returning to tuba after thirty years and joining Jazz Limited
summary: Chops never left; Jackson recommended him for a New Year's gig.

story.theme_name: Still working: current gigs, upcoming projects and plans
story.community_name: Managers, bookers and the business of getting work

blocks.x: Right. Well, when you finally dropped tuba, you eventually went back to it. Did you keep your chops up on tuba, or did you just put it in the closet for a few years?
Put it in the closet for a few years. And, in fact, it was about 30 years to be exact, about.
How'd you get your chops back so

well? They never left. That's what surprised me. Yeah, well, there was a friend of mine, trumpet player also, that I went to school with. Was organizing the Elks band. And he wanted me to come in on tuba. And I said, well, I don't know, I haven't played tuba in 30 years. I don't know whether I'd be able to make it or not. He said, well, you come in and get started. You might as well. I said, okay. So I made my first rehearsal, he found an old sousaphone, and I made my first rehearsal and come to find out, my chops had never left. Same way they were 30 years ago.
You've got beautiful, beautiful teeth. Look like they're just made for a brass instrument. Probably helped do it.

The funny part about it, though, was when Franz Jackson recommended me to Bill -- Ruth and Bill Reinhart (PHONETIC), come in on tuba. I hadn't played it then in about -- that's about three or four years. It was longer than that since I played Dixieland. So she said, well, you think you can make it? I said, oh, yeah, I can make it. So what I did was I got all different records, played along with the phonograph to try to see if I had that swing beat again. Come to find out, I said, yeah, I can play all the tunes again. I just went around -- I went in
On New Year's Eve. For a one-night gig. Wound up 12 years at Jazz Limited.
